query: For initially solid iron–nickel–chromium–cobalt–copper high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles examined across the premelting and melting regime, limited understanding of their thermal response constrains interpretation of application limits and high-temperature synthesis, where cooling must consolidate the solid solution. Prior studies of Ag, Au, Al, and Pd nanoparticles established that nanoscale phase-transition behavior can differ markedly among particle systems, but findings from single-metal particles do not resolve the response of chemically complex nanoparticles. Work on bimetallic particles further demonstrated that chemical complexity can produce varied configurations, while research on high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles remains sparse and has not established the governing physics for this composition. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its premelting and melting behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline particle, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, prior findings that support it, and an observation that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The onset of premelting in equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed by thermodynamically driven surface segregation of Cu, which forms a low-melting, Cu-rich shell that nucleates surface melting at a temperature substantially below that of a compositionally homogeneous particle of the same size.
generation.material_initial_state: ∼10 nm equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles synthesized to be chemically random at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Controlled in situ heating from 600 K to 1200 K under vacuum during aberration-corrected TEM combined with spatially resolved EDS mapping.
generation.conditions: Particle diameter 5–20 nm; equiatomic composition within ±5 at %; heating rate 10 K/min; high vacuum (≤10⁻⁵ Pa).
generation.structural_mediator: Surface segregation of Cu leading to a Cu-rich shell.
generation.mechanism: Cu has the lowest bulk melting point and surface energy in the alloy; at elevated T it migrates to the surface, forming a liquid-like shell that lowers the overall premelting temperature by reducing the surface energy barrier to melting.
generation.predicted_outcome: Particles exhibiting Cu-enriched surfaces will show the first signs of surface melting (liquid layer formation and morphological fluctuations) at ≈100 K lower than compositionally homogeneous (no-segregation) particles of the same size.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic nanoparticles processed to suppress Cu surface segregation (e.g., rapid quench from synthesis) showing no detectable Cu enrichment at the surface prior to heating.
generation.boundary: Applies to equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles 5–20 nm in diameter under inert or vacuum conditions; not tested for particles >20 nm, non-equiatomic alloys, or in reactive atmospheres.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of melting point depression estimated (±50 K); actual segregation extent and kinetics may vary with particle size and synthesis history.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of ∼10 nm equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles: (1) annealed at 600 K to induce Cu surface segregation (confirmed by EDS), and (2) rapidly quenched to suppress segregation. Perform in situ TEM heating with EDS mapping.
measurements: Temperature of first observable surface liquid layer (premelting onset) via real-time diffraction/contrast changes
Surface composition profiles before and during heating via EDS line scans
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both sets exhibit indistinguishable premelting onset temperatures within ±20 K and/or if the Cu-segregated sample does not exhibit a measurable Cu-rich surface prior to melting, then the hypothesis is falsified.
